cues.text: Let us close this study session by consolidating what you need to be able to do in an exam.
Think of this chapter as a checklist of abilities, and I will walk through each one in the order the source gives them.
First, you must be able to explain architecture versus implementation.
Architecture is the high-level structure of a system: its major parts and how they relate to one another.
Implementation is the actual building of those parts, the code and configuration that make the structure real.
In an answer, show that you can keep the two apart, and say which decisions belong to each.
Second, patterns and trade-offs.
You should be able to explain design and architectural patterns, and, importantly, that every choice has trade-offs.
A pattern is not simply good or bad.
You must say what it gives you and what it costs you.
Third, UML and ERD.
UML, the Unified Modeling Language, is used to model systems visually.
ERD stands for entity-relationship diagram, which models data entities and the relationships between them.
Be ready to explain what each diagram shows and when you would use it.
Fourth, code quality.
Be able to explain what makes code good, and how that quality is maintained.
Fifth, the Git workflow.
Explain how a team uses Git to manage changes to code.
Sixth, debugging and logging.
Debugging is finding and fixing faults.
Logging is recording what the system does, so that faults can be investigated.
Seventh, secure design.
Explain how security is built into a system's design rather than added afterwards.
Eighth, measured performance.
Notice the word measured.
Performance claims should rest on measurement, not on assumption.
Now the second sentence of the source, which tells you how to reason in an answer.
Choose architecture for actual business constraints.
In other words, do not pick a fashionable architecture and then defend it.
Start from the real constraints of the business, and select what fits them.
Then justify three things.
One: data ownership, meaning which part of the system owns which data.
Two: failure behaviour, meaning what happens when a part of the system fails.
Three: operational complexity, meaning how hard the system is to run, deploy, and maintain.
A strong answer names all three and connects them to the business constraints.
Finally, the security principle.
Security requires layered controls.
No single control is enough.
And the source gives a precise example: a successful login does not permit access to every record.
Authentication, proving who you are, is only one layer.
The system must still check, for each record and each action, whether that particular user is allowed to see or change it.
Remember that sentence, because it is an easy and very common exam point.
